messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan is a 33-year-old prosecutor who came to treatment after more than a year of trying to force himself back into a life that, from the outside, still looked intact. He is married, known at work for being composed in court, and had prided himself before the attack on being someone who could think clearly under pressure. The event that now organizes so much of his inner life happened on an ordinary weekday evening after he had left the courthouse and stopped at a crowded downtown restaurant to meet a colleague. He remembers noticing a group at the bar, the smell of spilled liquor and beer hanging in the room, and then a violent blast that seemed to split the space apart. Even now, when he tries to describe it, the account breaks up. He can say there was a bang, then heat, then screaming, then people on the floor, but when he tries to put the sequence together he loses it. He has told his wife that it is like holding shards instead of a story.

What is clear to him is the sense that there was a moment in which something terrible might still have been stopped if he had moved faster, shouted sooner, pulled someone down, done anything more than what he did. He remembers seeing people looking around in confusion just before the explosion and has come to fix on that instant with merciless scrutiny. In his mind, he was the one who should have recognized danger, should have protected people, should have acted. He does not talk about this as a vague regret. He says it as a verdict: he failed. He will sit with his jaw clenched and say that other people were injured and he walked out alive, and that he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened.

In the weeks afterward, Ethan returned to work quickly, partly because the routines of prosecution felt like the only thing in his life that still had rules. But the world no longer seemed populated by ordinary people. In courthouse hallways, in elevators, in the coffee line, he found himself studying faces with a hard, suspicious attention. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that danger could sit unnoticed in plain sight until the second it declared itself. He did not say this dramatically; it showed up in small, relentless ways. He watched hands, bags, jackets, the timing of someone stepping too close. If a stranger lingered in the back of a courtroom, Ethan tracked him instead of listening fully to testimony.

His symptoms are tied to specific moments in his daily life. Because the attack happened after a long workday, exhaustion has become one of the states he fears most. When he is very tired, especially after long trial preparation or late nights reviewing files, his guard feels thinner and the memory comes in harder. He has learned to dread that drained, heavy feeling in his body because it seems to leave him less able to keep the scene away. The smell of alcohol is another immediate jolt. Passing by the courthouse bar association events, walking through a restaurant with his wife, or catching whiskey on someone’s breath in a crowded elevator can stop him cold. He does not simply remember the attack then; for a few moments it feels present, as if the room around him has been overrun by that earlier room. Loud bangs are worst of all. Construction noise near the courthouse, a slammed metal door, a car backfiring outside chambers—his body reacts before he can think, and the explosion is there again with a vividness that feels more real than normal memory, sharper and more convincing than what is actually in front of him.

What troubles Ethan almost as much as the intrusions is that he cannot make the event into a coherent narrative. He can deliver an airtight chronology in court, but when the subject is the bombing, his own mind refuses sequence and order. He moves from the smell of alcohol, to the flash, to someone on the ground, to his own useless hesitation, and then says he cannot trust any of it because it comes in fragments that feel too alive. At home, his wife has tried to ask what happened, but he often stops after a sentence or two, frustrated and ashamed. Over time he has withdrawn from dinners out and from work gatherings where drinks are served. He has stayed later in his office to avoid joining colleagues, and his wife has noticed how often he insists on quieter routes, quieter restaurants, quieter evenings.

He sought help after a recent incident outside the courthouse when a sudden booming sound from nearby construction brought the whole scene back with such force that he had to brace himself against a wall. He was shaken not only by the intensity of it, but by the fact that it happened in the middle of the workday, in the professional setting where he has tried hardest to appear untouched. He says he is afraid that if this continues he will become someone who cannot trust anyone, cannot be with his wife in ordinary places, and cannot carry the responsibility of his job without constantly scanning for catastrophe. At the same time, what he hopes for is simple and painful in its simplicity: to be able to remember what happened as something that happened, not something that keeps arriving again, and to live without the constant conviction that he failed everyone who was there.
